newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia picks Rolls-Royce engines for Hawks.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia picks Rolls-Royce engines for Hawks.

text.p: The Australian Defence Department said on Wednesday it had selected Rolls-Royce Plc to supply engines for its order for up to 40 British Aerospace Hawk attack-trainer aircraft.

The decision ends AlliedSignal Inc's hopes that the Royal Australian Air Force (RAAF) would launch its F124 engine on the Hawk, a big-selling trainer currently supplied only with Rolls-Royce's Adour engine.
Rolls said in a statement on Wednesday it would supply the Adour Mark 871, the standard engine offered on the current Hawk models.
The RAAF said last year it wanted to look at fitting the AlliedSignal engine because it had a number of apparent advantages, including weight and ease of maintenance.
Australian defence sources said Rolls had responded to the challenge by detailing an upgrade of the Adour that could be implemented in a few years.
The upgrade would substantially close the technology gap between the British and U.S. engines, one source said.
"The first 12 Adour engines for (Australian Hawks) will be supplied by Rolls-Royce Military Aero Engines Ltd's Bristol facility in England," Rolls said.
Qantas Airways Ltd would assemble and test the remaining engines. Qantas would then be responsible for maintaining the engines in service.
Australian Defence Minister Ian McLachlan said both engines would have been met requirements but Rolls had been selected after exploring the cost and risk trade-offs between the two.
The exact number of the Australian Hawk order will depend on final negotiations with British Aerospace this year.
This was AlliedSignal's second attempt to displace Rolls from the Hawk.
The U.S. Navy version of the Hawk, the McDonnell Douglas-built T-45 Goshawk, was tested with the U.S. engine last year. But the engine was removed from the test aircraft after just one flight.
Analysts had speculated that an Australian order for the F124 would have launched a new-generation Hawk model.
Australia is buying the Hawks under its Lead-In Fighter project to replace elderly Aeromacchi MB.326 trainers.
British Aerospace has sold more than 700 Hawks since the aircraft was first developed for Britain's Royal Air Force in the 1970s.
